opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things I find most exciting about the model. A big refactor is less about writing clever code and more about persistence and staying coherent over a long stretch of work. You have to hold a mental map of the codebase, make a change in one place, see what breaks somewhere else, and keep iterating without losing the thread.

We trained GPT-5 Codex specifically on that kind of real-world engineering work. Not just isolated puzzles, but tasks where you have to navigate a large repository, run the tests, read the failures, and adjust. What emerges is a model that's much better at what I'd call sustained effort. It doesn't give up after the first attempt, and it doesn't declare victory early. It checks its own work, and if something's off it goes back and fixes it.

Part of it is that the model is more adaptive in how it spends its thinking. For a quick question it answers quickly. When it recognizes a really hard, multi-step task, like untangling a big module or migrating an API across dozens of files, it's willing to keep going for a long time, sometimes hours, steadily working through the problem. Internally we've seen it run on tasks for a very long time and still be making meaningful progress at the end, which honestly surprised us at first.

The way I think about it, it's starting to feel less like an autocomplete and more like a teammate you can hand a substantial piece of work to. You come back later and the job is actually done, with tests passing and a clear explanation of what changed. That shift from "help me write this function" to "go take care of this refactor" is really what we're excited about.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we actually spent a lot of time thinking about, because a big refactor is really the hardest case for an agent. It's not one clever insight. It's hours of unglamorous, careful work where you have to hold the whole shape of the change in your head and not lose the thread.

The way I think about it is that there are really three things going on. The first is just that the model has gotten much better at planning and then sticking to the plan. When you give it a large refactor, it'll break it down, it'll figure out the order of operations, and it keeps a sense of where it is in that sequence. Earlier models would do the first few steps well and then kind of drift, or they'd declare victory too early. GPT-5 Codex is much more willing to keep going until the thing is actually done.

The second piece is that it uses the tools to verify itself. It doesn't just make edits and hope. It runs the tests, it runs the build, it greps for the remaining call sites, and when something breaks it goes back and fixes it rather than papering over it. That feedback loop is what lets it make real progress instead of just producing a lot of diffs. And one thing we saw in training is that the model got noticeably better at knowing when it's on the right track versus when it needs to back up and reconsider.

And then the third thing, which I think is underrated, is how it manages its own effort. We've seen it work for many hours on a single task, but it's not spending that time uniformly. On the simple parts it moves fast, and on the parts that are genuinely tricky, it slows down, reads more code, and reasons more carefully. So it's dynamically allocating its thinking depending on the difficulty, which is really what a strong engineer does too.

So when people ask how it keeps making progress, my honest answer is that it's less about one capability and more about the combination. Persistence on the plan, tight verification loops, and knowing where to spend the effort. When those come together, you get an agent that you can hand a messy, multi-file refactor to, walk away, and come back to something that actually works.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-5 Codex can plan and persist through a refactor to completion, but describes it creating its own plan; it does not state that it carries the refactor through after receiving an initial plan.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a complex refactor isn’t one decision. It’s a sequence of changes, where each change can reveal something you didn’t understand about the codebase. You need to inspect the code, make a change, run the relevant tests, and use that feedback to decide what to do next, while keeping the original goal in mind.

That’s how I’d think about the ability to keep making progress: can it stay in that loop? If a test fails, can it figure out whether it broke something or whether its understanding was wrong? Can it adjust without losing track of what the refactor was supposed to accomplish? The important thing isn’t just continuing to work for a long time. It’s making progress that you can verify.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as maintaining a loop: understand the code, make a change, check what happened, and use that feedback to decide what to do next. In a complex refactor, the first change often reveals more work—a dependency you missed, a failing test, or an assumption that no longer holds. The important capability is to keep working through those discoveries while staying focused on the original goal.

That doesn’t mean every step is correct. It means the model can recognize when an approach isn’t working, revise it, and continue. Tests and other checks give it concrete feedback, so progress comes from repeatedly connecting its reasoning to what the code actually does.
